title: Sorry, even store brands are expensive now

summary.headline: Cheapflation: Why budget-friendly groceries are rising in price
summary.tldr: Researchers have identified a phenomenon called cheapflation, where the prices of budget-friendly grocery items rise faster than premium products. This trend disproportionately affects low-income households, potentially erasing the benefits of government stimulus payments.

key_points.point: Cheapflation occurs when the prices of low-cost, budget-friendly goods increase at a higher rate than premium versions of the same products.
key_points.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that switching to store brands is a reliable way to escape the effects of high inflation.

key_points.point: Between January 2020 and May 2024, prices for cheaper food and beverages in the US rose 30%, while premium versions rose 22%.
key_points.why_it_matters: This data reveals that inflation is not experienced equally across all income levels or product categories.

key_points.point: Increased consumer demand for budget items during inflationary periods and the inability of low-margin companies to absorb rising costs drive this trend.
key_points.why_it_matters: Understanding these drivers helps explain why budget-friendly staples like rice and bread have become significantly more expensive.

key_points.point: Alberto Cavallo notes that the utility cost—the loss of satisfaction from being forced to switch away from preferred brands—is an additional burden for shoppers.
key_points.why_it_matters: It highlights that the impact of inflation goes beyond just the dollar amount spent, affecting the quality of life for consumers.

summary.lesson: When demand shifts toward lower-cost alternatives during economic stress, the increased volume can drive up prices for those specific goods, effectively reducing the purchasing power of the very consumers who rely on them most.
opinions_and_predictions: Alberto Cavallo (Harvard Business School) believes that for many low-income households, cheapflation erased the income gains provided by government stimulus payments during the pandemic.

glossary.definition: A phenomenon where the prices of budget-friendly, low-cost goods rise faster than the prices of premium goods.
glossary.example: Store-brand eggs increasing in price more rapidly than organic, name-brand eggs.

glossary.definition: The practice of reducing the size or quantity of a product while keeping the retail price the same.
glossary.example: A cereal box containing fewer ounces of product but sold at the same price as before.

glossary.definition: The economic concept of lost satisfaction or benefit when a consumer is forced to choose a less preferred product due to price constraints.
glossary.example: Having to buy a generic cottage cheese that one does not enjoy as much as the preferred brand.

glossary.definition: A total or summary statistic that combines many individual data points into one single figure.
glossary.example: Using a single inflation rate to represent price changes across an entire economy.

summary.quality_note: The report relies on academic research from Harvard Business School and the Bank of Canada, supplemented by anecdotal evidence from a food blogger.
